sections.overview: The Colorado potato beetle is a leaf beetle from North America that became one of the world’s most serious potato pests. It first fed on wild nightshades, moved onto cultivated potato in the 19th century, and later spread across Europe and Asia.
sections.identification: Adults are oval, dome-shaped and 8–10 mm long. Each wing cover bears five black stripes on a yellow ground, and the orange thorax carries black spots. Larvae are soft, plump and hump-backed, with a row of black spots along each side; the eggs are yellow-orange and about 1.7–1.8 mm long. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: It lives mostly in fields of potato and other nightshade crops such as tomato, eggplant and pepper, and on wild nightshades in grassland and suburbs. The species originated in the south-western United States and Mexico, spread east of the Rockies, and is now established across Europe, Asia Minor, Iran, Central Asia and China.
sections.diet: Adults and larvae both eat leaves, mainly of Solanum plants. Cultivated potato is the favourite host, ahead of eggplant, tomato, pepper and wild nightshades. A heavy attack can strip a plant down to stems.
sections.behavior: Adults and larvae are active by day and inactive at night. Adults can fly several kilometres, especially when crowded, and males release a pheromone that attracts both sexes. Larvae defend themselves by walking away, regurgitating and wiggling.
sections.reproduction: Adults overwinter in the soil, usually at field edges, and emerge in spring. Females lay clusters of yellow-orange eggs under leaves, up to about 800 in a lifetime. The larvae pass through four stages, then pupate in the soil, and a life cycle lasts about 30 days depending on temperature. There are two or three generations a year, and some adults stay in the soil for more than one winter.
sections.ecology: Fungi, predatory insects, toads and birds attack the beetle, but they rarely control it alone. Its resistance to insecticides is a major issue: more than 300 cases have been documented in Asia, Europe and North America.
sections.conservation: The species is not threatened; Animal Diversity Web lists its IUCN status as Not Evaluated. It is better known as an agricultural pest, and Great Britain fought three invasions in 1876, 1901 and 1914 with chemical control.
